patent: Filed October 24, 1962 and issued April 5, 1966 to Robert N. Hall of Schenectady, N.Y., assigned to General Electric. It claims the semiconductor injection laser: a forward-biased junction between degenerately doped N and P regions of a direct-gap compound such as gallium arsenide, with two faces polished flat and parallel, perpendicular to the junction, so that the crystal itself is the resonant cavity and the pump is a current pulse. Hall's group at the General Electric Research Laboratory reported pulsed laser emission from GaAs junctions at 77 K in Physical Review Letters (R. N. Hall, G. E. Fenner, J. D. Kingsley, T. J. Soltys and R. O. Carlson, "Coherent Light Emission From GaAs Junctions", vol. 9, p. 366, 1962), the work generally credited as the first semiconductor laser. GaAs junction lasers from IBM (M. I. Nathan et al.) and MIT Lincoln Laboratory (T. M. Quist et al.) followed in Applied Physics Letters within weeks; both are cited on the patent, as is the inversion condition of M. G. A. Bernard and G. Duraffourg (Physica Status Solidi, 1961) that FIG. 5 depicts. Nick Holonyak Jr. and S. F. Bevacqua, also of General Electric, reported visible emission from GaAsP junctions in 1962. These single-material (homojunction) devices needed current densities of thousands of amperes per square centimetre and pulsed, cooled operation; continuous operation at room temperature came in 1970 with double-heterostructure lasers (Zh. I. Alferov's group at the Ioffe Institute; I. Hayashi and M. B. Panish at Bell Laboratories). The edge-emitting geometry of FIG. 1, a junction stripe between two parallel end facets, is still the basic form of the laser diode.

figs.1: Perspective view of the diode. The crystal is a truncated block whose junction 4 runs horizontally, the P region 2 above it and the N region 3 below; top electrode 5 is soldered to the P side through layer 6 and base electrode 7 to the N side through layer 8, and strip connectors 9 and 10 bend down onto the two electrodes. Dashed lines are hidden edges, and a dashed leader points to a hidden face: 11 is the visible front face and 12 the hidden rear face, the polished parallel pair that forms the cavity and through which light leaves along the junction plane. Side faces 13 (visible) and 14 (hidden) lean inward, which gives the front face its trapezoid outline and keeps them from forming a second, transverse cavity. The underlined 1 has no leader and stands for the crystal as a whole.
figs.2: Drive circuit. Pulsed source 15 feeds the diode through series resistor 16; the diode symbol inside the dashed box is device 1, and the dashed box with arrow 17 is the temperature control enclosing it, which the text uses to set the threshold current (for example by immersing the diode in liquid air).
figs.3: Log-log plot of light output (arbitrary units, 1 to 100) against current density (10^3 to 10^5 A/cm^2). In region A the output follows a straight line, continued by the dashed line, and is incoherent spontaneous emission. At B, near 10^4 A/cm^2, the output rises steeply above that line: this is the lasing threshold. In C the rise slows again while the light stays coherent. The text says the output was measured perpendicular to front surface 11.
figs.4: Emission spectra, intensity in arbitrary units against wavelength in angstrom units (A.U.). The axis labels read 8200, 8400 and 8600, ticks every 100 A.U.; the hand-lettered 4 in the middle label resembles a 9. Broad curve D is the spontaneous emission below threshold, about 150 A.U. wide at half height per the text; narrow curve E is the emission above threshold, about 15 A.U. wide. The two curves are drawn to different vertical scales: the text puts the true peak of E at 20 to 50 times that of D. Both peak just above 8400 A.U., a photon energy of about 1.48 eV.
figs.5: Energy-level diagram across the junction under strong forward bias: energy upward, position left to right. On the degenerate N side (left) electrons fill the conduction band from its edge (the lower boundary of the upper hatched region) up to the top line; on the degenerate P side (right) the valence band is empty from its edge (the line above EMPTY STATES) down to the hatched region. In the inversion region in the middle, filled conduction states lie directly above empty valence states; the vertical arrows are the downward electron transitions that emit photons, each spanning at least the band gap E_{g} marked at left.
figs.6: Cylindrical variant, with numerals as in FIG. 1. From left: rod connector 9, end-disc electrode 5, solder ring 6, region 3, junction 4 drawn as a thin ring around the cylinder, region 2, solder ring 8, end electrode 7 and rod connector 10. The junction is a disc across the cylinder, and the text has the standing wave run across it radially, with light leaving through the curved side. The leaders here put region 3 beside solder 6 and region 2 beside solder 8, the reverse of the pairing in FIG. 1.
figs.7: Coaxial variant, seen from one end. Electrode 5 is a rod along the axis; around it, from the inside out, are solder 6, P region 2, junction 4 as a thin hollow cylinder, N region 3, solder 8 and the outer collar electrode 7. The cavity is the annular junction itself; the text has radiation leave through its ring-shaped ends, one of which is the concentric ring face in front.

parts.1: Drawn underlined, without a leader; the text describes the crystal as "indicated generally at 1" and later calls it diode 1.
parts.4: The gain region: per the text about 300 to 20,000 angstrom units thick, preferably about 500 to 2000. The text also allows it to be an epitaxially grown I-type layer, giving a P-I-N structure.
parts.11: Polished optically flat and parallel to rear surface 12 (about 0.1 micron in the GaAs example) or produced by cleaving; the text gives a reflectance of the order of 0.4 and allows partial metallizing or external mirrors.
parts.13: Cut to a taper, or alternatively roughened, so that no transverse standing wave forms between the side faces.
parts.14: Cut to a taper, or alternatively roughened, so that no transverse standing wave forms between the side faces.
parts.17: The text cools the GaAs diode to lower the threshold: about 10,000 A/cm^2 at 77 K and less than 2000 A/cm^2 at 20 K.

glossary.def: Emission of a photon by an excited electron, triggered by an incident photon of the same energy; the new photon has the same frequency, phase and direction, so the light builds up coherently.
Light whose waves keep a fixed phase relation in time and across the beam, as from a laser, rather than the random phases of spontaneous emission.
A state in which more electrons occupy the upper level of a transition than the lower one, so stimulated emission outweighs absorption and light is amplified.
Doping so heavy that the Fermi level lies inside the conduction band (N-type) or valence band (P-type), as the patent defines it; the semiconductor then behaves partly like a metal.

In current terms a direct-band-gap semiconductor, such as GaAs: the lowest conduction-band state and the highest valence-band state have the same crystal momentum, so electrons and holes recombine efficiently by emitting light.
A semiconductor made of an element from group III of the periodic table (gallium, indium) and one from group V (arsenic, phosphorus, antimony), such as GaAs or InP.
The energy separation between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band; it sets the photon energy, and so the wavelength, of band-to-band emission.

A pair of parallel reflecting surfaces between which light makes many passes, forming standing waves at wavelengths where a whole number of half wavelengths fits the spacing. Two parallel facets of the crystal are now called a Fabry-Perot cavity.
The drive current at which gain from stimulated emission overcomes the losses of the cavity and lasing starts, seen as the knee of FIG. 3.
The spectral width of an emission line measured at half its peak intensity, now usually called full width at half maximum (FWHM).
10^-10 m, 0.1 nm; 8400 angstrom units is 840 nm, in the near infrared.

Microwave amplification by stimulated emission of radiation; the microwave predecessor of the laser. Three- and four-level masers and lasers are pumped through auxiliary levels, unlike the directly current-pumped diode here.
An excited state with an unusually long lifetime, where pumped electrons accumulate to give the inversion in three- and four-level lasers.
The average distance an injected electron in P material, or hole in N material, travels before recombining; the patent uses it to bound the thickness of the junction region.
Absorption of light by mobile electrons or holes moving within their band; a loss that competes with gain in heavily doped material.
A diode with an undoped or lightly doped (intrinsic, I) layer between its P and N regions.
A vacuum-insulated flask for cryogenic liquids.
